picks.style: ancient mystery-cult processional, double aulos and frame drums, lead cantor answered by massed voices, incantatory, torchlit, building
picks.why: 'I charge them once, I charge them twice, I charge them thrice' — a mystic chorus with the repetition already written into it.

picks.style: anacreontic drinking song, lyre and light hand percussion, warm tenor, lilting, convivial, unhurried
picks.why: Ennius's Anacreontic — no shield, no Pleiads, just a deep cup with vines carved on it. A complete little song.

picks.style: latin lyric miniature, solo cithara, intimate close-mic voice, hushed, rubato, suspended
picks.why: The soul climbing to the lips during a kiss and nearly escaping — the most beautiful thing in the whole compilation.

picks.style: roman comic canticum, double tibia and hand drum, blustering baritone, strutting march tempo, mock-heroic
picks.why: The braggart's opening boast about his dazzling shield and homesick sabre — the play's signature and instantly funny.

picks.style: patter comic song, tibia and plucked strings, fast wry male voice, breathless, escalating, farcical
picks.why: The wife waking him before cockcrow — 'give me some money, my dear' — a rant that builds like a chorus.

picks.style: temple invocation, soft aulos and finger cymbals, clear female voice, slow, sweet, ceremonial
picks.why: Fire on the altar and Arabian smoke for Diana of Ephesus — a genuine lyric moment inside the farce.

picks.style: english pastoral art song, piano and cello, gentle tenor, slow, tidal, elegiac
picks.why: A whole sonnet, storm to stillness, ending on melodies that mourn upon the lyre and expire as they mourn.

picks.style: ethereal choral lullaby, harp and glassy layered voices, weightless, floating, refrain-driven
picks.why: 'Come, rest with us! evanishing, they cried — Come, rest with us! the lonely vale replied' — the refrain is already there.

picks.style: gothic ballad, low strings and harp, dramatic mezzo, hushed then opening out, slow release
picks.why: Terror pointing forever at a stony coffin, then the prisoner released into the smell of spring — one clean turn.

picks.style: restoration theatre song, harpsichord and baroque violin, rakish tenor, dance lilt, teasing
picks.why: 'I love thee well, but not so well to wed thee' — a real stage song with short lines built for a tune.

picks.style: english catch in parts, tavern voices in rounds, fiddle and tabor, boisterous, quick, communal
picks.why: A catch sung in parts, opening on 'there's no man grows old till he ceases to drink'.

picks.style: scotch-air ballad, fiddle and small pipes, plain tenor, brisk, wry, cold-morning
picks.why: Set to a Scotch tune by the author himself; the lad making his moan alone on a winter morning.

picks.style: solemn baroque death-ode, string orchestra and muted brass, grave baritone, slow, measured, funereal
picks.why: 'Yes, Death is ever at my hand, fast by my bed he takes his stand, and constant at my board is found.'

picks.style: martial elegy, timpani and low strings, declamatory bass, processional, darkening, abrupt close
picks.why: The world's victor vanishing like a morning cloud, 'allow'd to fight, to conquer, and to die' — written by a king.

picks.style: prussian court ode, horns and harpsichord, resolute tenor, stately, defiant, storm-driven
picks.why: Voltaire may retire to Plato; the writer must be 'in thought, in life, in death a king'. A perfect closing line.

picks.style: georgian parlour song, harpsichord and cello, light soprano, gentle triple time, tender
picks.why: Four 'twas nots and then the turn — 'No — 'twas your generous nature' — anaphora made for singing.

picks.style: english pastoral air, flute and guitar, warm mezzo, flowing, sunlit, hymn-like
picks.why: Love as the breeze in a calm and the drop that sparkles in the eye — a short song of pure images.

picks.style: 18th century emblem song, viol and harpsichord, bright arch soprano, dainty, stepwise, witty
picks.why: The rose like a coquette, the tulip like an empty beau — a flower-emblem catalogue that actually has jokes.

picks.style: latin tragic recitative, solo lyre over a low drone, grave male voice, slow, incantatory, receding
picks.why: Only candidate; the regress of wishes — no felled firs, no tree, no Mount Pelion at all — reads as a built chain.

picks.style: english pastoral ode, horn and harpsichord, measured baritone, stately, shadowed, unhurried
picks.why: Only candidate; it opens on 'breathes a browner horror o'er the woods', which is worth the song by itself.
